name: Tripeptide-10 citrulline

lead: Tripeptide-10 citrulline, sold as Decorinyl, is a cosmetic peptide modeled on decorin, a molecule that organises collagen fibres. It is used in anti-wrinkle products for tidier collagen and firmer, smoother skin.

It is designed to bind collagen the way decorin does, regulating fibril diameter and cohesion. In vitro work reported thinner, more uniform collagen fibres. A 24-person randomized study of its combination with acetyl hexapeptide-3 reported measurable changes in skin microtopography and transepidermal water loss. Clinical data are small and mostly in combination.

paras: It is used in anti-aging serums and creams, often in combination with other peptides, as part of a daily routine. Texture changes in the small study were measured over a short period of regular use.
The published abstracts do not report adverse effects. Safety data beyond these studies were not found. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Tripeptide-10 citrulline (Decorinyl) mimics decorin to organise collagen fibres, aiming for firmer, smoother skin. In vitro data show more uniform fibres, and one 24-person randomized study of a combination reported changes in skin microtopography.

lead: Tripeptide-10 citrulline (marketed as Decorinyl) is a synthetic peptide used in anti-aging skin care to make skin look smoother and firmer by supporting orderly collagen fibres. It is designed to mimic the collagen-binding behaviour of decorin, a small proteoglycan that helps regulate how collagen fibrils form, so cosmetic users apply it in the hope of fewer visible wrinkles and better skin texture.[1][2][3]

The 2008 report that described it argued that functional decorin declines as skin ages, leaving collagen fibres disrupted and tensile strength reduced, so a decorin substitute could make up the difference. Its authors identified tetrapeptide candidates from decorin's collagen-binding sites, screened them in a collagen fibrillogenesis assay, and found that tripeptide-10 citrulline regulated fibril diameter in vitro.[1] They describe it as targeting collagen quality rather than quantity.[1]

A 2017 randomized study of 24 volunteers tested the peptide with and without acetyl hexapeptide-3 and measured skin microtopography and transepidermal water loss.[2] Wikipedia describes decorin as a collagen-binding proteoglycan that influences fibril formation.[3]
infobox: In vitro fibrillogenesis assay (2008); 24-person randomized study (2017)[1][2]

paras: Decorin binds collagen and limits excessive bundle-like aggregation. The authors of the 2008 report argued that decorin function declines with age. They engineered tetrapeptide candidates from decorin's collagen-binding sites and screened them in a collagen fibrillogenesis assay; tripeptide-10 citrulline performed best and regulated fibril diameter in vitro, producing thinner and more uniform fibres.[1] Wikipedia describes decorin as a small proteoglycan binding type I collagen fibrils and influencing fibrillogenesis and matrix assembly.[3]
Tripeptide-10 citrulline appears in anti-aging products, often alongside other peptides such as acetyl hexapeptide-3, which was the other active in the 2017 study.[2]

A prospective randomized controlled study enrolled 24 healthy volunteers across four groups: the two peptides combined, each alone, or neither, for 60 days. Skin microtopography parameters and transepidermal water loss were measured with a skin visioscan and tewameter, with significant between-group differences at several time points.[2] The authors concluded the results supported antiwrinkle activity of acetyl hexapeptide-3 and provided clinical evidence for tripeptide-10 citrulline, while noting that the mechanism of any synergy was unclear.[2] The sample was small.

timeline.event: A decorin-like tetrapeptide for organising collagen fibres is described, including tripeptide-10 citrulline.[1]
A randomized study of its combination with acetyl hexapeptide-3 is published.[2]
